T Max ( T a, T b )

## Slide 11
**Function Templates: Incomplete Instantiation**

Use Power template as follows:

```cpp
template < unsigned N, typename T >
T Power ( T v )
{
    T res = v;
    for ( int i=1; i<N; i++ )
        res *= v;
    return res;
}

void main()
{
    double d1 = Power<5>(1.2);
    double d2 = Power<5,int>(1.2);
    std::cout << d1 << " " << d2;
}

    Why result values of d1 and d2 are different? Hint: type conversions!

    Slide 12

    Function Template Instantiation Kinds

    template < typename T1, typename T2 >
void F ( T1 v1, t2 v2 )
{
    . . .
}

    F<int,float>(v1,v2); Complete explicit instantiation; all template actual types are taken directly from the instantiation.

    F<int>(v1,v2); Incomplete explicit instantiation; some actuals are taken from the instantiation, other actuals are deduced from the call’s actual types.

    F(v1,v2); Implicit instantiation; all template actuals are deduced from the call’s actual types.

    Slide 15

    Explicit Specializations (3)

    Generic form:

    template<typename T>
class C {
    public: bool less ( T& v1, T& v2 )
    {
        return v1 < v2;
    }
}

    Special form: explicit specialization

    template<>
class C<const char*> {
    public: bool less ( const char* v1, const char* v2 )
    {
        return strcmp(v1,v2)<0;
    }
}

    Slide 17

    Explicit Specializations: Summary

    1. It is possible to specify explicit specialization(s) for a template for special cases of template argument(s).
    2. The implementation of explicit specialization may differ from the implementation of the “primary” template.
    3. All explicit specializations of a template together with the “primary” template itself form the single family of classes.
    4. All cases of use of either “primary” template or its explicit specializations are processed during compile time.

{

    // implementation
}

    From the primary template, an orange dashed arrow points left to a box labeled C<int>. The text reads: “The act of instantiating the class template: template instantiation”. This leads to:

    template<>
class C<int>
{
    // Instantiated
    // “primary”
    // implementation
}

    This is labeled “Explicitly instantiated template specialization” and categorized under “Classes-by-template (non-standard)”.

    From the primary template, another orange dashed arrow points right, accompanied by the text “(Explicit) declaration of template specialization”. This leads to:

    template<>
class C<char*>
{
    // An alternative
    // implementation
    // for the concrete type
}

    This is labeled “Explicitly specialized template specialization” and categorized under “Template specializations”.]

    Slide 19

    Explicit Specializations: Example (1)

    One more example: Factorial

    N! = 1 for N=0 N! = 1 for N=1 N! = N * (N-1) * … 2 * 1 for N>=2

    Obvious implementation: recursive function:

    unsigned long Fact ( unsigned N )
{
    if ( N<2 ) return 1;
    return N*Fact(N-1);
}

    How to use this function? Which problems can occur?

    int x = 8;
unsigned long f1 = Fact(x);
unsigned long f2 = Fact(5);

    19/30

    Slide 20

    Explicit Specializations: Example (2)

    Let’s try to make a “template” version of Fact. The first (straightforward) attempt:

    template < unsigned N >
unsigned long Fact ( void )
{
    if ( N<2 ) return 1;
    return N*Fact<N-1>();
}

    What will happen while instantiating the template? unsigned long f5 = Fact<3>();

    20/30

    Slide 21

    Explicit Specializations: Example (3)

    How it works[Image Description: A diagram visualizing infinite compile-time recursion when expanding the recursive template without a base specialization. A call to unsigned long f5 = Fact<3>(); instantiates Fact<3>, which internally calls Fact<3-1>(). A red arrow links this to the instantiation of Fact<2>, which calls Fact<2-1>(). Another red arrow links this to Fact<1>, which calls Fact<1-1>(). The sequence continues to Fact<0>, calling Fact<0-1>(), accompanied by the text “…And so on!” indicating an infinite loop.]

    template<>
unsigned long Fact<3> ( void )
{
    if ( 3<2 ) return 1;
    return 3*Fact<3-1>();
} 

template<>
unsigned long Fact<2> ( void )
{
    if ( 2<2 ) return 1;
    return 2*Fact<2-1>();
} 

template<>
unsigned long Fact<1> ( void )
{
    if ( 1<2 ) return 1;
    return 1*Fact<1-1>();
} 

template<>
unsigned long Fact<0> ( void )
{
    if ( 0<2 ) return 1;
    return 0*Fact<0-1>();
}

    template < unsigned N >
unsigned long Fact ( void )
{
    return N*Fact<N-1>();
}

    Primary template N! = N*(N-1)!

    template<>
unsigned long Fact<0> ( void )
{
    return 1;
}

    Explicit specialization for N=0 0! = 1

    template<>
unsigned long Fact<1> ( void )
{
    return 1;
}

    Explicit specialization for N=1 1! = 1

    Slide 3

    Functional Objects & Templates (1)

    Problem: Find the first array element which is equal to a given value. Solution:

    const int* find1 ( const int* pool, int n, int x )
{
    const int* p = pool;
    for ( int i = 0; i < n; i++ )
    {
        if ( *p == x ) return p; // success
        p++;
    }
    return 0; // fail
}
```[Image Description: In the code block above, a red circle highlights the hardcoded equality check `*p == x` inside the `if` statement.]

Example of use:
```cpp
int A[100];
. . .
int* p = find1(A,100,5); // p points to the 1st element of A
                         // which is equal to 5, or p==0.

    3/38

    Slide 4

    Functional Objects & Templates (2)

    More general problem: Find the first array element which satisfies a condition. Solution:

    const int* find2 ( const int* pool, int n, bool (*cond)(int) )
{
    const int* p = pool;
    for ( int i = 0; i < n; i++ )
    {
        if ( cond(*p) ) return p; // success
        p++;
    }
    return 0; // fail
}
```[Image Description: Arrows highlight parts of the code indicating the use of a function pointer callback. 
An arrow points to `bool (*cond)(int)` in the function parameters, labeled "Pointer to function calculating the condition". 
Inside the loop, `cond(*p)` is circled in red, and an arrow from a box labeled "Call by pointer" points directly to it.]

Example of use:
```cpp
int A[100];
bool cond_eq5 ( int x ) { return x == 5; }
int* p = find2(A,100,cond_eq5);// p points to the 1st element of
                               // A which is equal to 5, or p==0.

. . .
bool cond_range_0_100 ( int x )
{
    return (x >= 0) && (x <= 100);
}
int* p2 = find2(A,100,cond_range_0_100);

    Well-known example: qsort() function from the Std library:

    void qsort ( void* base,     // first element
             size_t num,     // number of elements

    Slide 6

    Functional Objects & Templates (4)

    Summary: the general principle of the technique: Passing the pointer to a callback function containing the expression on the array element.

    Callback function: pros & cons: :) Flexible and general mechanism: we can specify (virtually) any condition; :( Inefficient: repeated code generates a lot of overhead (while the expression the callback function evaluates is typically very simple); :( Inefficient: slows down pipelined machines (function calls force the processor to stall).

    Slide 7

    Functional Objects & Templates (5)

    The ideal solution should be: :) Flexible and general as callbacks; :) More efficient than callbacks.

    The basis for the better solution: • Classes with user-defined call operators; • Templates!

    Slide 13

    Functional Objects & Templates (9)

    Generic find3() version:

    template < typename T, typename Comparator >
T* find3 ( T* pool, int n, Comparator comp )
{
    T* p = pool;
    for ( int i = 0; i < n; i++ )
    {
        if ( comp(*p) ) return p; // success
        p++;
    }
    return 0; // fail
}

    Advantages: • The function searches arrays of any type (no requirements) • The function can search values by any criteria • It is more efficient than the original find2() version![Image Description: Red annotations show how the hardcoded elements from the previous slide are now generalized. Arrows link the text “any type” to the generic T* parameter. Arrows link the text “any criteria” to the Comparator comp parameter and comp(*p) call, which are circled in red.]

    Another way to organize a set of predicates like comparators:

    template < typename T >
class Compare
{

    The general comparator

    template < typename T >
class Positive {
public:
    bool operator()(T x)const { return Compare<T>()(0,x); }
};
```[Image Description: Text "Adapter" points to the `Positive` class. A pop-up box illustrates the logic behind `Compare<T>()(0,x);`: `Compare<T> c; return c(0,x);` The code `Compare<T>()(0,x)` is circled in red.]

{

};

## Slide 17
**Functional is the Trend!**

Almost every modern programming language has at least some “functional” features.

• C++: lambda expressions, function types, functions without side effects, type inference
• C#: function types (“delegates”), function literals, type inference
• Java 8: lambda expressions
• Swift: functions as values; closures; local functions
• Rust: functions as variables, as arguments, as return values; anonymous functions

17/38

## Slide 18
**Functional Programming (1)**

The common philosophy in functional programming:
The program functionality is implemented as a (great) number of functions (“building blocks”), each of which performs relatively simple action on its arguments returning the result (without side effect).

There are three basic ways for programming functions (C++)… and one more:
• Define a function as an object member.
• Define function as a class member (“static”)
• Define a standalone function.
• Define a function as an object!

18/38

## Slide 19
**Functional Programming**

Two cornerstones of functional approach:
• Immutable objects
• Functions as “first-class citizens”

19/38

## Slide 20
**FP 1: Immutable Objects**

Data are immutable:
The operations of a program should map input values to output values rather than change data in place.

Or: Methods should not have any side effects. They should communicate with their environment only by taking arguments and returning results… For any given input the method call could be replaced by its result without affecting the program’s semantics.

Advantages:
• Programs are easy-for-testing.
• Programs are verifiable.
• Programs can be parallelized.

20/38

## Slide 21
**FP 2: Functions as Objects**

Functions are values – just as integers, arrays etc.
• Function is an abstraction of an operation.
• Define functions anywhere (just as other variables).
• “Constant” (or unnamed, or anonymous) functions are allowed (like integer constants).
• Functions can be assigned, passed as arguments to other functions etc.

    Lambdas: Return Type

    [](int x) { return x+1; } If the lambda body contains the single return statement then (and only then) the return type can be deduced by the compiler

    [](int& x) { ++x; } Otherwise, the return value is assumed to be void

    [](int x)->int { cout<<“Hi!”; return x+1; } If the lambda body contains more than one statement then the return type had to be specified explicitly before C++14. But no longer required

    [] { return sizeof(int); } If no parameters then () can be omitted

## Slide 31
**Lambdas & Closures**

Notation for lambda capture:

`[a, &b]` a gets captured by immutable value, b gets captured by reference
`[&]` the whole context gets captured by reference
`[=]` the whole context gets captured by immutable value
`[=, &a]` the whole context gets captured by immutable value except a that is captured by reference
`[*this]` this pointer gets captured by value
`[this]` this pointer gets captured by reference
`[]` nothing is captured from the context

3  int bytes = sizeof(x); // passing an object
4  return bytes / 4 + (bytes % 4 > 0);
